titleEn: Greenfield Robotics opens public share offering after 6 years in the field
titleZh: Greenfield Robotics 田间运营六年后启动公开募股
summaryZh: 美国堪萨斯州 Greenfield Robotics 在商业化运营六年后，通过 StartEngine 平台启动 Regulation A+ 公开募股，目标融资最高 1860 万美元。该公司生产机械除草自主机器人，采用无人机测绘+机器人执行的分离式架构，目前已有 82 台机器人在 16 个州的付费客户田间作业。公司计划将自主平台扩展至施肥、覆盖作物播种、覆盖作物覆盖及主作物种植等四项新任务，并与 Amity Technology 建立制造合作以实现规模化生产。
featuredReason: Greenfield Robotics 的公开募股是农业机器人商业化的重要里程碑，其“无人机测绘+地面机器人执行”的分离式架构、从除草向多任务平台的扩展路径，以及从按使用付费转向直接销售的商业模式演变，对智慧农业从业者理解自主机器人落地逻辑和商业化节奏具有重要参考价值。

Photos: Greenfield Robotics Greenfield has 82 robots operating in paying customers’ fields across 16 states. Photos: Greenfield Robotics US company Greenfield Robotics has opened its ownership to everyday investors, aiming to raise up to $18.6 million (€16.3 million) through a Regulation A+ offering on StartEngine. Shares are priced at $2.07 (€1.82) each, and the offering is open to both accredited and non-accredited US investors, as well as international investors. The Kansas-based company builds autonomous robots that cut weeds mechanically, with the aim of replacing herbicides. The public offering comes six years after its first machines began working commercial crop fields. As of publication, more than $428,000 (€376,000) has already been raised through the offering. Greenfield now has 82 robots operating in paying customers’ fields across 16 states. Its 2026 season sold out, delivering more than $1 million (€880,000) worth of robots, and the company already counts around 2,600 shareholders from earlier funding rounds. The system separates seeing the field from working it. A drone first maps where weeds sit relative to the crop rows, producing a digital prescription; the company’s BOTONY robot then follows that map and cuts weeds mechanically at ground level, without chemicals. Greenfield plans to extend the same autonomous platform beyond weeding next season, adding four further tasks: feeding crops after dark, seeding and mulching cover crops, and planting the cash crop itself. !Image 7: Each robot runs on two swappable lithium-ion batteries, good for three to three-and-a-half hours before they need roughly the same amount of time to recharge. Each robot runs on two swappable lithium-ion batteries, good for three to three-and-a-half hours before they need roughly the same amount of time to recharge. What it costs and how it performs Each robot runs on two swappable lithium-ion batteries, good for three to three-and-a-half hours before they need roughly the same amount of time to recharge, either by pulling the batteries out or charging them in place through a port on the machine. Greenfield currently quotes a working rate of about 0.85 acres per hour. In a pilot at the University of Vermont a single robot covered around seven acres a day. According to Greenfield’s Nathan Dyrud in US media, each robot costs $36,500 (€32,100). His rule of thumb is one machine for every 80 to 100 acres of row crops, meaning a 200-acre grower would likely need 2 or 3 robots, and a 300-acre operation 3 or 4. The company has also shifted its commercial model. It has moved away from the pay-per-use service it once offered, under which farmers could hire the robots for a season without committing to a purchase, toward outright sales; a lease option is said to be coming later but has not yet been detailed. !Image 8: A key part of the growth story behind the offering is Greenfield's manufacturing partnership with Amity Technology, a Fargo, North Dakota-based equipment maker. A key part of the growth story behind the offering is Greenfield’s manufacturing partnership with Amity Technology, a Fargo, North Dakota-based equipment maker. A personal starting point Founder Clint Brauer, a third-generation farmer from outside Wichita, Kansas, has said the company grew out of his father's diagnosis with Parkinson's disease. “My dad got Parkinson’s. That began the quest”, he said. Brauer had spent 14 years working in technology in Los Angeles before returning to the family farm and beginning work on a mechanical alternative to the herbicides his family had sprayed for decades. The offering lands at a moment of mounting legal and regulatory pressure on the herbicides Greenfield’s robots are designed to replace. Combined with growing herbicide resistance among weeds, growers are increasingly choosing between heavier chemical applications, more tillage, or manual labour – the gap Greenfield is positioning its robots to fill. !Image 9: Greenfield plans to extend the same autonomous platform beyond weeding next season, adding four further tasks: feeding crops after dark, seeding and mulching cover crops, and planting the cash crop itself. Greenfield plans to extend the same autonomous platform beyond weeding next season, adding four further tasks: feeding crops after dark, seeding and mulching cover crops, and planting the cash crop itself. Manufacturing at scale A key part of the growth story behind the offering is Greenfield's manufacturing partnership with Amity Technology, a Fargo, North Dakota-based equipment maker. “For a long time, we made these by hand in a shed in Kansas”, Brauer said. “There's a production line in Fargo now. That changes how fast we can put machines out and how fast we can iterate on them.” North Dakota has committed $500,000 (€439,000) toward a dedicated production facility for the work. Greenfield’s robots have also found their way into research settings: Cornell University and the University of Wisconsin have purchased units for research purposes, while the University of Nebraska won a grant to do the same. The US Department of Agriculture has run Greenfield’s fleet at Grand Farm in North Dakota, the agency’s robotics site within its National Proving Grounds Network for AgTech. Investors and partners in the company include Chipotle’s Cultivate Next fund, KingsCrowd Capital, the Rodale Institute and the Kansas Department of Commerce. Ahead of the offering's official launch, more than 500 prospective investors indicated interest in reserving over $1 million (€880,000) worth of shares during the company's "testing the waters" period – non-binding expressions of interest rather than confirmed commitments. Proceeds from the raise are earmarked for manufacturing and production, field operations, research and development, and general company costs. translationZh:
美国公司 Greenfield Robotics 已向普通投资者开放所有权，旨在通过 StartEngine 平台上的 Regulation A+ 发行筹集最高 1860 万美元（1630 万欧元）。每股定价 2.07 美元（1.82 欧元），该发行面向美国合格和非合格投资者，以及国际投资者开放。这家总部位于堪萨斯州的公司制造自主机器人，通过机械方式除草，目标是替代除草剂。此次公开募股距离其首批机器开始在商业化作物田间作业已有六年。截至发稿时，该发行已筹集超过 42.8 万美元（37.6 万欧元）。Greenfield 目前有 82 台机器人在 16 个州的付费客户田间运行。其 2026 季已售罄，交付了价值超过 100 万美元（88 万欧元）的机器人，公司在此前融资轮次中已拥有约 2600 名股东。该系统将“感知田间”与“作业田间”分离。无人机首先测绘杂草相对于作物行的位置，生成数字处方图；然后公司的 BOTONY 机器人按照该地图行进，在地面高度以机械方式切割杂草，不使用化学品。Greenfield 计划在下一季将同一自主平台扩展到除草之外，增加四项任务：夜间为作物施肥、播种和覆盖覆盖作物，以及种植主作物本身。

**成本与性能**

每台机器人使用两块可更换的锂离子电池，续航三到三个半小时，之后需要大致相同的时间充电，可以取出电池或将机器通过端口就地充电。Greenfield 目前标称作业效率约为每小时 0.85 英亩。在佛蒙特大学的一次试点中，单台机器人每天覆盖约七英亩。据 Greenfield 的 Nathan Dyrud 在美国媒体上所述，每台机器人售价 36,500 美元（32,100 欧元）。他的经验法则是每 80 到 100 英亩大田作物配备一台机器，这意味着一个 200 英亩的种植者可能需要 2 到 3 台机器人，300 英亩的经营者需要 3 到 4 台。公司还调整了商业模型。它已从曾经提供的按使用付费服务——农民可以租用机器人一个季度而无需承诺购买——转向直接销售；据说租赁选项将在稍后推出，但尚未详细说明。

**个人起点**

创始人 Clint Brauer 是堪萨斯州威奇托郊外的第三代农民，他表示公司源于他父亲被诊断出帕金森病。“我父亲得了帕金森病。这开启了探索之旅”，他说。Brauer 在洛杉矶从事科技工作 14 年后回到家族农场，开始研究一种机械替代方案，以取代他家几十年来喷洒的除草剂。此次发行正值 Greenfield 机器人所旨在替代的除草剂面临日益增大的法律和监管压力之际。加之杂草对除草剂的抗性不断增强，种植者越来越多地在更重的化学施用、更多的耕作或人工劳动之间做出选择——这正是 Greenfield 将其机器人定位填补的空白。

**规模化制造**

此次发行背后增长故事的关键部分是 Greenfield 与 Amity Technology 的制造合作，后者是总部位于北达科他州法戈的设备制造商。“很长一段时间，我们是在堪萨斯州的一个棚子里手工制造这些机器的”，Brauer 说。“现在法戈有了生产线。这改变了我们推出机器的速度以及迭代的速度。”北达科他州已承诺投入 50 万美元（43.9 万欧元）用于专门的生产设施。Greenfield 的机器人也进入了研究领域：康奈尔大学和威斯康星大学已购买设备用于研究目的，内布拉斯加大学获得了拨款做同样的事。美国农业部已在北达科他州 Grand Farm 运行 Greenfield 的机队，该农场是该机构在农业科技国家验证基地网络中的机器人基地。公司的投资者和合作伙伴包括 Chipotle 的 Cultivate Next 基金、KingsCrowd Capital、Rodale Institute 和堪萨斯州商务部。在发行正式启动之前，超过 500 名潜在投资者在公司“试探水温”期间表示有兴趣预留价值超过 100 万美元（88 万欧元）的股份——这些是非约束性的意向表达，而非确认承诺。募集资金指定用于制造和生产、田间运营、研发以及一般公司费用。
contentHtml: Greenfield Robotics opens public share offering after 6 years in the field US company Greenfield
